title: Don't-Care Conditions
excerpt: Some input combinations can never happen. Marking them X instead of 0 lets your groups grow through them, and often removes a whole term from the answer.
seoTitle: Don't-Care Conditions in Karnaugh Maps Explained
seoDescription: What don't-care conditions are, where they come from, and how marking impossible inputs as X instead of 0 shrinks the simplified expression. With a worked BCD example.

content.text: Up to now every cell in the map has been a 0 or a 1. Real circuits have a third case: input combinations that cannot occur at all, so their output genuinely does not matter.

These are don't-care conditions, written X on the map, and they are not a shortcut or an approximation. They are a statement that the specification never says what should happen for that input, which leaves you free to pick whichever answer makes the circuit smaller.
The most common source is a code that does not use its full range, like a four-bit field that only ever carries the digits 0 through 9.

rows: Binary-coded decimal: 4 bits holding one decimal digit
A one-hot signal where exactly one line is high
Every combination with two or more high
A state machine with unreachable states
Any encoding no transition can produce

content.text: In each case the hardware will never see those inputs, so forcing the output to 0 there is a choice, and usually a needlessly expensive one.

body.text: Worked example: is the digit 5 or more?

content.text: Four bits ABCD carry one BCD digit, so only 0000 through 1001 ever appear, and the output should be 1 when the digit is 5 or more, which means minterms 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9.
First, the cautious version. Treat the six impossible inputs as 0, because that feels safe, and see what the map gives you.
That gives A'BD + A'BC + AB'C', three terms and nine literals, because every group is boxed in by the zeros sitting around it.
Now mark those six as don't-cares instead, and watch what the groups do.
Now it is BD + BC + A, three terms and five literals. Same circuit behavior for every input that can actually happen, built from noticeably less logic.
The groups were able to expand into the X cells because nothing stops them there, and a group is only illegal if it covers a 0.

rows: Yes, by at least one group

content.text: That middle row is the one to internalize: a don't-care is worth including when it enlarges a group, and worth ignoring when it does not, which is a judgment call the solver makes for you every time it draws a boundary. A group made entirely of don't-cares is legal but pointless. It covers nothing that needed covering.

Don't-care means the input cannot occur, not that you have not thought about it. Those are very different claims, and confusing them produces a circuit that behaves arbitrarily on inputs that turn out to be reachable after all.
If a malformed input is merely unlikely rather than impossible, it is not a don't-care. Decide what should happen and write that down as a 0 or a 1, because the extra gate is cheaper than the bug.
This map has don't-cares in it. Group it yourself, then check whether you used them to your advantage.

questions.prompt: What does an X in a Karnaugh map mean?

options.label: That input combination cannot occur, so the output for it does not matter
The output is unknown and should be treated as 0
The cell has not been filled in yet

questions.prompt: May a group include a don't-care cell?

options.label: Yes, whenever including it makes the group larger
Only if the group is otherwise all don't-cares

questions.prompt: You form a group made entirely of don't-cares. What is wrong with it?

options.label: It covers no 1s, so it adds a term to the expression without doing any work
It is illegal and the map cannot be solved
Nothing, it is a useful simplification
